title: NVIDIA is about to start taking a share of cloud providers' revenue.
text:
It has been reported that, in an effort to break the monopoly of tech giants, NVIDIA is providing financial guarantees for emerging cloud providers by offering GPU computing capacity lease-back arrangements to address their financing challenges. In exchange, NVIDIA will take a revenue share from these cloud providers, directly participating in profit distribution in the downstream computing market and extending its control further down the industrial chain.
NVIDIA is leveraging its strong balance sheet to gain market leverage, quietly evolving from a chip vendor into the 'central bank' of the AI computing ecosystem by offering financial backing to emerging cloud service providers in exchange for a share of their revenue.
On July 1, according to the technology news outlet The Information, NVIDIA is providing financial guarantees to young cloud service providers that lease or rent its GPUs—if these companies fail to secure enough AI developers to rent their computing capacity, NVIDIA will repurchase their unsold GPU capacity at a pre-agreed price.
In return, NVIDIA will receive a percentage of these cloud providers’ revenue, with the revenue-sharing rate gradually declining over the term of the contract. GPU cloud providers Firmus and Sharon AI have already joined the program, and three executives with existing business ties to NVIDIA confirmed the arrangement.
On July 1, NVIDIA published a statement on its official website announcing a new business model that combines revenue sharing with credit support, enabling AI cloud providers to procure NVIDIA infrastructure without bearing the full upfront capital expenditure, and allowing them to offer computing services to downstream AI-native enterprises, model developers, and corporate clients.
According to the report, the initiative is internally referred to by some NVIDIA personnel as the 'AI Compute Partnership.' A NVIDIA spokesperson also confirmed the existence of the program. This move marks a significant strategic shift for NVIDIA:
On one hand, it lowers financing barriers for emerging cloud service providers to expand its customer base; on the other, it directly participates in profit distribution within the downstream computing market through revenue sharing, thereby extending its control further down the AI value chain.
Business Model Shift: From Selling Chips to Sharing Cloud Revenue
According to NVIDIA’s official press release, the company will earn not only standard product revenue but also an additional share of cloud service revenue, creating a usage-based, recurring revenue stream. The core objective of this model is to overcome the long-standing financing barrier that has constrained startups from accessing large-scale computing power.
NVIDIA positions this framework as the 'DSX AI Factory' model, targeting AI service scenarios requiring continuous cross-regional operations, high utilization rates, and multi-tenant accelerated computing.
Sharon AI and Firmus are the first cloud providers participating in this model. Sharon AI plans to deploy up to 40,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs, while Firmus is constructing a DSX AI Factory campus in Batam, Indonesia, expected to scale up to 360 megawatts and accommodate up to 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs. These deployments directly reflect NVIDIA’s latest progress in transforming computing demand into deployable, financeable infrastructure.
NVIDIA noted that emerging AI companies have historically faced significant constraints in accessing capital-intensive infrastructure—even long-term contractual commitments have often been insufficient to secure financing for compute capacity procurement. This means that numerous AI-native firms, model developers, and inference service providers face lengthy delays when scaling their computing capabilities: site selection, power procurement, construction, and hardware commissioning—each step can take several months or even longer.
The promise of this new model is to realign economic structures so these groups can rapidly access full-stack accelerated computing capabilities without waiting for the traditional infrastructure build-out cycle to complete.
Underlying Rationale: Addressing the Core Challenge of GPU Financing
Reportedly, GPUs typically represent the most expensive component in AI data centers. For chip buyers with lower credit ratings, securing sufficient loans is itself a major hurdle.
A data center executive commented on such NVIDIA deals as “killing two birds with one stone.” He explained that if NVIDIA merely provided a guarantee for a data center facility lease, “you’d still face the question of ‘how to finance the GPUs’”; but if NVIDIA commits to purchasing any unsold compute capacity within the facility, “the GPU financing issue is resolved—and so is the data center’s financing problem.”
In other words, NVIDIA’s backstop commitment effectively serves as a credit enhancement tool, enabling emerging cloud service providers—who would otherwise struggle to obtain bank loans—to mobilize significantly larger amounts of capital and accelerate data center construction.
Strategic Intent: Breaking the Dominance of Large Customers
NVIDIA’s launch of these initiatives is grounded in a clear strategic context. Currently, a small number of large cloud service providers—including Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Meta, and Google—purchase the majority of NVIDIA’s chip output. However, several of these companies are developing their own competitive AI chips, posing a potential threat to NVIDIA.
To reduce its reliance on these giant clients, NVIDIA has spent the past few years actively supporting a cohort of emerging GPU cloud service providers, such as CoreWeave. The newly announced 'AI Compute Partnership Program' represents a continuation and deepening of this strategy.
According to prior reporting by The Information, NVIDIA has also recently been negotiating to provide financial guarantees for OpenAI’s lease of a large data center in Ohio—an asset that, if fully built out at current prices for chips, labor, power, and other materials, could cost as much as $500 billion.
Capital Commitments: From Equity Investments to Capacity Guarantees
NVIDIA’s capital commitments in this direction have already become substantial.
To date, NVIDIA has invested several billion dollars in equity stakes in multiple emerging cloud service providers and, in certain cases, agreed to lease back chips from these companies—including CoreWeave and Lambda—in transactions totaling several billion dollars. According to prior reporting by The Information, NVIDIA’s own researchers have also used GPU servers leased back from Lambda.
On the capacity guarantee front, NVIDIA began advancing related deals in the autumn of last year. In September 2024, NVIDIA committed to purchasing all of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity through 2032 if CoreWeave failed to secure tenants, under a contract then valued at $6.3 billion. This move effectively alleviated investor concerns about CoreWeave’s highly leveraged business model and drove its stock price up nearly 30% within the following week.
According to a regulatory filing submitted by NVIDIA in May of this year (covering the quarter ended in April), NVIDIA subsequently added another $3.5 billion to guarantee customer data center leases in exchange for rights to purchase their shares.
Taken together, NVIDIA is constructing a multi-layered mechanism to align interests: equity investments, capacity leasebacks, lease guarantees, and now revenue-sharing arrangements. Each layer deepens the financial ties between NVIDIA and downstream cloud service providers, enabling NVIDIA to directly share in the incremental returns from the commercialization of AI computing power beyond chip sales alone.
